title: Chile, Peru and Argentina
notes: Chile's CEFAA, Peru's office and the Argentine cases.

lead.text: Chile created an open, civil-aviation office for anomalous aerial phenomena in 1997, CEFAA, now SEFAA, which after a dormant spell from 2002 to 2008 still runs and publishes its resolved cases; Peru's Air Force reopened an office of its own in 2013; and an Argentine airliner case of 1995 surfaced in the 2026 US file release.

summary.text: Chilean official reporting began in 1968, when Aviation Colonel Sergio Bravo Flores, head of the Meteorological Office, led a commission that asked 43 aeronautical installations for reports and sent some of them to the University of Colorado study later known as the Condon Committee.

After sightings at Arica in 1997, the head of Chile's civil aviation directorate, the DGAC, created CEFAA on 3 October 1997 at its technical school in Santiago; in 2021 it was renamed SEFAA and placed under the DGAC's communications subdepartment. Its stated mission is to support the safety of air operations.
Peru's Departamento de Investigacion de Fenomenos Aereos Anomalos, DIFAA, sits inside the Peruvian Air Force; it reopened in October 2013 after five years closed.

The best-known Chilean case is the Navy helicopter infrared footage of November 2014, which CEFAA analysed for two years and released in January 2017; the Argentine case is Aerolineas Argentinas flight AR 674 at Bariloche on 31 July 1995.

record.text: The DGAC's own history names General Gonzalo Miranda Aguirre as the director who created CEFAA by resolution in 1997, with Colonel Enzo Di Nocera as its first director, prompted by the Arica sightings and the interest of a former Chilean Air Force commander in chief.
The office's remit is the safety of air operations across the DGAC's area of responsibility, some 32 million square kilometres from Arica to the South Pole.

By September 2021 CEFAA had received 1,675 cases, with 362 arriving in 2020, nearly 300% above earlier years, supported by a digital database created in 2018. In 2018 it consisted of its director, Hugo Camus Palacios, and two investigators, with an external committee of scientists, controllers, pilots and engineers.

Since 2020 the office has published its investigated and resolved cases, with yearly indexes from 2018 and monthly bulletins still appearing in 2026; the DGAC describes it as one of the oldest public bodies of its kind on the continent and as leading a model of transparency.
The DGAC records a gap: from 2002 to 2008 CEFAA entered a period of latency, and it was reactivated by resolution in December 2009.

Canada's Sky Canada Project named Chile, with the United States and France, as the models worth examining, described SEFAA as the official Chilean body for collecting and studying UAP inside the civil aviation directorate, and recommended partnership with it.

Peru's state news agency reported DIFAA's reopening on 18 October 2013, announced by Colonel Julio Vucetich Abanto of the Air Force's space directorate in response to rising sightings reported in the media, and said it brought Peru level with Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Brazil and Ecuador.
At the meeting where the reopening was announced, the invited archaeologist said there is no evidence linking the Nazca lines to UFOs or extraterrestrial presence.

claimed.text: Press accounts of the Navy footage say the helicopter crew tracked the object from about 40 miles, got no reply to repeated calls, and that two radar stations could not see it although they could see the helicopter; controllers said no aircraft was authorised in the area.
CEFAA's director Ricardo Bermudez summed up its finding on the Navy case by saying that it did not know what the object was, only what it was not.

The Bariloche case is described in a file in the May 2026 US Department of War release of more than 160 files, including a double airport power failure and a go-around; press reports say the file sits in a section on foreign investigations and references the French COMETA report.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said of the release that the files, hidden behind classification, had long fuelled justified speculation; within days it produced an Argentine national story and a Japanese government review.

On the board's reading, Chile's long run of an open office that releases military footage shifts the burden onto anyone who says public handling of UAP data would cause unacceptable harm, and its 2017 release preceded the US authorisation of the Navy videos by more than three years.

contested.text: The Navy footage was not left unexplained by everyone: French analysts brought in through GEIPAN proposed an airliner venting cabin wastewater, which CEFAA rejected, and independent analysts later matched the footage to scheduled flights LA330 and IB6830.

The DGAC's own records disagree about who ran CEFAA: one passage says Bermudez directed it from 1997 to 2016, while the directorship chronology gives Di Nocera to 1998, Bermudez to 2002, Hernan Henriquez Cobaise to 2008, and Bermudez again from 2009 to 2016.

The two regional offices are built on opposite models: DIFAA sits inside an air force and said it would share data with neighbours only exceptionally, while SEFAA sits in a civil aviation authority and treats the subject as aviation safety. The board has not established DIFAA's founding instrument, its current reporting line or whether it publishes any findings.

questions: Which was it: did Bermudez run CEFAA continuously from 1997, or with a gap while others held the post?
Why did CEFAA fall dormant from 2002 to 2008, and what was lost in that time?
Did CEFAA ever answer the flight-match explanation of the 2014 Navy footage?
Under what instrument was Peru's DIFAA founded, why was it closed for five years, and has it published any case findings since 2013?
What does the US file on the Bariloche case contain beyond what the press has reported, and where did the US obtain it?
Are Bravo Flores's Chilean reports among the Condon Committee's surviving papers?
